column3: C1: Understands key ideals and principles of the United States, including those in the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, and other foundational documents.

column4: Explain key ideals and principles outlined in the Declaration of Independence, including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness; the U.S. Constitution, including the rule of law, separation of powers, representative government, and popular sovereignty; and, the Bill of Rights, including due process and freedom of expression.
column5: Explaining America's founding ideals
column12: Exemplary — You explain what the founding ideals mean and show how they connect to each other.
column14: Proficient — You explain what key ideals like liberty, rule of law, and due process mean, using the documents.
column16: Progressing — You name founding ideals but explain only some of them, or mix them up.
column18: Beginning — You can list words from the documents but not say what they mean yet.

column4: Evaluate efforts to reduce discrepancies between key ideals and reality in the United States.
column5: Judging how far America has closed the gap between promise and reality
column12: Exemplary — You judge how much an effort closed the gap between an ideal and real life, and weigh what it did and didn't fix.
column14: Proficient — You judge how well an effort closed the gap between an American ideal and real life, using evidence.
column16: Progressing — You describe an effort and the gap, but you don't judge how well it worked.
column18: Beginning — You name an ideal or a problem without connecting the two yet.

column3: C2: Understands the purposes, organization, and function of governments, laws, and political systems.

column4: Analyze the structure and powers of government at the national level.
column5: Analyzing how the national government is built
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how the branches are built and powered, and explain how their powers depend on each other.
column14: Proficient — You analyze the structure of the national government and what powers each part holds.
column16: Progressing — You name the branches and some powers, but the analysis stays general.
column18: Beginning — You can name parts of the government but not what they do yet.

column4: Use knowledge of the function of government to analyze and address a political issue.
column5: Using how government works to tackle an issue
column12: Exemplary — You analyze an issue using how government works, and propose a step that fits the part of government that can actually act.
column14: Proficient — You use what you know about how government works to analyze a political issue and suggest a response.
column16: Progressing — You describe the issue, but you don't connect it to how government works.
column18: Beginning — You state an opinion on the issue without using how government works yet.

column4: Evaluate the effectiveness of the system of checks and balances in the United States based on an event.
column5: Judging whether checks and balances worked
column12: Exemplary — You judge how well checks and balances worked in an event, and weigh more than one view of the result.
column14: Proficient — You judge how well checks and balances worked in a real event, using evidence from it.
column16: Progressing — You describe the event and name a check, but you don't judge how well it worked.
column18: Beginning — You can name checks and balances but not apply them to an event yet.

column4: Demonstrate that the U.S. government includes concepts of both a democracy and a republic.
column5: Showing the U.S. is both a democracy and a republic
column12: Exemplary — You show where the government is democratic and where it is a republic, and explain why it was built with both.
column14: Proficient — You show, with examples, how the U.S. government works as both a democracy and a republic.
column16: Progressing — You define the terms but give examples for only one of them.
column18: Beginning — You can name the terms but not show them in the government yet.

column3: C3: Understands the purposes and organization of tribal and international relationships and U.S. foreign policy.

column4: Identify early examples of foreign policy between the United States and other nations.
column5: Identifying early U.S. foreign policy
column12: Exemplary — You identify early foreign policy examples and explain what the young nation was trying to protect.
column14: Proficient — You identify early examples of how the United States dealt with other nations.
column16: Progressing — You name an event involving another country but not the policy behind it.
column18: Beginning — You can name other countries but not how the U.S. dealt with them yet.

column4: Analyze how the United States has interacted with other countries.
column5: Analyzing how the U.S. deals with other countries
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how the U.S. interacted with another country, and explain how both sides were affected.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how the United States interacted with another country, using evidence.
column16: Progressing — You describe an interaction but stop before explaining why it happened or what changed.
column18: Beginning — You name countries the U.S. dealt with without explaining how yet.

column4: Analyze how a claim on an issue attempts to balance individual rights and the common good.
column5: Analyzing rights versus the common good
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how a claim balances individual rights and the common good, and explain what it costs each side.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how a claim tries to balance individual rights with the good of everyone.
column16: Progressing — You name the rights or the common good, but you don't show the balance between them.
column18: Beginning — You give an opinion on the issue without weighing rights against the common good yet.

column4: Employ strategies for civic involvement that address a national issue.
column5: Taking civic action on a national issue
column12: Exemplary — You use a strategy for civic action and explain why it fits this issue and this audience.
column14: Proficient — You use a real strategy for civic involvement to address a national issue.
column16: Progressing — You name a way to get involved but don't connect it to the issue.
column18: Beginning — You describe a national issue without a plan to act on it yet.

column3: E1: Understands that people have to make choices between wants and needs and evaluates the outcomes of those choices.

column4: Analyze examples of how groups and individuals have considered profit and personal values in making economic choices in the past or present.
column5: Analyzing money-versus-values choices
column12: Exemplary — You analyze an economic choice and explain how profit and personal values pulled against each other.
column14: Proficient — You analyze an economic choice, showing how profit and personal values shaped it.
column16: Progressing — You describe the choice but account for only profit or only values.
column18: Beginning — You name an economic choice without explaining what shaped it yet.

column3: E2: Understands how economic systems function.

column4: Analyze how the forces of supply and demand have affected the production, distribution, and consumption of goods, services, and resources in the United States in the past or present.
column5: Analyzing supply and demand
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how supply and demand changed what was made, moved, or bought, and trace the chain of effects.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how supply and demand affected what was produced, sold, or used.
column16: Progressing — You define supply and demand but apply them only loosely to the example.
column18: Beginning — You name a product or a price without connecting it to supply and demand yet.

column4: Analyze how the forces of supply and demand have affected international trade in the United States in the past or present.
column5: Analyzing supply and demand in trade between nations
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how supply and demand shaped trade between nations, and explain who gained and who lost.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how supply and demand affected U.S. trade with other countries.
column16: Progressing — You describe trade between countries without showing supply and demand at work.
column18: Beginning — You name traded goods without explaining what drove the trade yet.

column3: E3: Understands the government’s role in the economy.

column4: Analyze the influence of the U.S. government’s taxation, creation of currency, and tariffs in the past or present.
column5: Analyzing taxes, money, and tariffs
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how taxes, currency, or tariffs changed people's lives, and explain who they helped and who they hurt.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how a government decision about taxes, money, or tariffs affected the economy.
column16: Progressing — You describe a tax or a tariff without showing its effects.
column18: Beginning — You can name taxes, currency, or tariffs but not their impact yet.

column3: E4: Understands the economic issues and problems that all societies face.

column4: Analyze the distribution of wealth and sustainability of resources in the United States.
column5: Analyzing who has wealth and whether resources last
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how wealth and resources are shared, and explain what makes the pattern hold or change.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how wealth is spread out and whether resources can last.
column16: Progressing — You describe wealth or resources but not the pattern in how they're shared.
column18: Beginning — You name rich and poor groups without analyzing the pattern yet.

column4: Explain the costs and benefits of trade policies to individuals, businesses, and society in the United States.
column5: Explaining what trade policies cost and give
column12: Exemplary — You explain the costs and the benefits of a trade policy, and show they land differently on different groups.
column14: Proficient — You explain both the costs and the benefits of a trade policy for people, businesses, or society.
column16: Progressing — You explain either the costs or the benefits, not both.
column18: Beginning — You name a trade policy without its costs or benefits yet.

column3: G1: Understands the physical characteristics, cultural characteristics, and location of places, regions, and spatial patterns on the Earth’s surface.

column4: Explain and analyze physical and cultural characteristics of places and regions in the United States.
column5: Explaining what makes a place what it is
column12: Exemplary — You analyze the physical and cultural features of a region, and explain how they shape each other.
column14: Proficient — You explain and analyze the physical and cultural features of a U.S. place or region.
column16: Progressing — You describe features of a place but treat physical and cultural ones separately.
column18: Beginning — You name places without describing what makes them different yet.

column4: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions and their political, cultural, and economic dynamics.
column5: Reading maps to explain why location matters
column12: Exemplary — You use maps and images to explain how location shaped politics, culture, or money, and you notice what the map leaves out.
column14: Proficient — You use maps, images, or other sources to explain how a place's location affects life there.
column16: Progressing — You read information off a map but don't connect location to what happens there.
column18: Beginning — You can find places on a map but not explain why location matters yet.

column3: G2: Understands human interaction with the environment.

column4: Analyze how the environment has affected people and how people have affected the environment in the United States in the past or present.
column5: Analyzing how people and the environment change each other
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how the environment shaped people and how people changed the environment, and you connect the two directions.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how the environment affected people and how people affected the environment.
column16: Progressing — You analyze one direction of the relationship, not both.
column18: Beginning — You name an environmental feature without connecting it to people yet.

column4: Explain cultural diffusion in the United States from the past or in the present.
column5: Explaining how culture spreads
column12: Exemplary — You explain how a cultural practice spread, and what changed about it along the way.
column14: Proficient — You explain how a cultural practice, idea, or product spread from one group to another.
column16: Progressing — You name cultures in contact but don't trace what spread.
column18: Beginning — You name cultural practices without explaining how they traveled yet.

column4: Explain and analyze migration as a catalyst for the growth of the United States in the past or present.
column5: Analyzing how migration grew the country
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how migration drove growth, and explain what it cost the people who moved and the people already there.
column14: Proficient — You explain and analyze how migration helped the United States grow.
column16: Progressing — You describe people moving without connecting it to growth.
column18: Beginning — You name groups who migrated without explaining the effect yet.

column3: G3: Understands the geographic context of global issues and events.

column4: Explain how learning about the geography of the United States helps us understand global issues such as diversity, trade, and sustainability.
column5: Connecting U.S. geography to global issues
column12: Exemplary — You explain how U.S. geography helps make sense of a global issue, and where the comparison breaks down.
column14: Proficient — You explain how learning U.S. geography helps you understand a global issue like trade, diversity, or sustainability.
column16: Progressing — You describe a global issue without connecting it to geography.
column18: Beginning — You name global issues without linking them to place yet.

column4: Explain how themes and developments help to define eras in United States history from 1763 to 1877, including: Fighting for independence (1763-1783); Establishing the new nation (1781-1815); Slavery, expansion, removal, and reform (1801-1850); Civil War and Reconstruction (1850-1877)
column5: Explaining what makes an era an era
column12: Exemplary — You explain what defines an era, and show where one era bleeds into the next.
column14: Proficient — You explain how themes and events define an era in U.S. history between 1763 and 1877.
column16: Progressing — You place events in time but don't explain what ties an era together.
column18: Beginning — You can name events without placing them in an era yet.

column3: H2: Understands and analyzes causal factors that have shaped major events in history.

column4: Explain and analyze how individuals and movements have shaped United States history (1763-1877).
column5: Analyzing how people and movements changed history
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how a person or a movement changed history, and weigh how much they changed against what was already moving.
column14: Proficient — You explain and analyze how an individual or a movement shaped U.S. history.
column16: Progressing — You describe what a person or movement did without showing what changed because of it.
column18: Beginning — You name people or movements without their impact yet.

column4: Explain and analyze how cultures and cultural and ethnic groups have contributed to United States history (1763-1877).
column5: Analyzing what different groups contributed
column12: Exemplary — You analyze what a cultural or ethnic group contributed, and explain why that contribution is often left out.
column14: Proficient — You explain and analyze how a cultural or ethnic group shaped U.S. history.
column16: Progressing — You name a group’s contribution without analyzing its effect.
column18: Beginning — You name groups without their contributions yet.

column4: Explain and analyze how technology and ideas have impacted United States history (1763-1877).
column5: Analyzing how technology and ideas changed history
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how a technology or an idea changed history, and follow effects people didn't expect.
column14: Proficient — You explain and analyze how a technology or an idea changed U.S. history.
column16: Progressing — You describe a technology or an idea without showing what it changed.
column18: Beginning — You name inventions or ideas without their impact yet.

column3: H3: Understands that there are multiple perspectives and interpretations of historical events.

column4: Analyze and interpret historical materials from a variety of perspectives in United States history (1763-1877).
column5: Reading history from more than one perspective
column12: Exemplary — You interpret sources from several perspectives, and explain why the same event looks different to each.
column14: Proficient — You analyze historical sources from more than one perspective.
column16: Progressing — You read sources but stay inside one perspective.
column18: Beginning — You retell what a source says without asking whose view it is yet.

column4: Analyze multiple causal factors to create positions on major events in United States history (1763-1877).
column5: Taking a position using more than one cause
column12: Exemplary — You take a position using several causes, and judge which mattered most and why.
column14: Proficient — You analyze more than one cause of a major event and take a position based on them.
column16: Progressing — You name causes but your position rests on only one.
column18: Beginning — You state a position without causes behind it yet.

column3: H4: Understands how historical events inform analysis of contemporary issues and events.

column4: Analyze how a historical event in United States history helps us to understand contemporary issues and events.
column5: Using the past to understand today
column12: Exemplary — You analyze how a past event helps explain an issue today, and name where the comparison stops working.
column14: Proficient — You analyze how an event in U.S. history helps you understand an issue happening now.
column16: Progressing — You connect past and present, but the link stays on the surface.
column18: Beginning — You describe a past event without connecting it to today yet.

column3: SSS1: Uses critical reasoning skills to analyze and evaluate claims.

column4: Analyze positions and evidence supporting an issue or an event.
column5: Analyzing positions and the evidence behind them
column12: Exemplary — You analyze a position and its evidence, and explain how it argues against other positions.
column14: Proficient — You analyze a position and the evidence given for it, using specifics from the source.
column16: Progressing — You describe a position and mention evidence, but you don't separate the two.
column18: Beginning — You retell what a source says without finding the position yet.

column4: Evaluate the logic of reasons for a position on an issue or event.
column5: Judging whether reasons hold up
column12: Exemplary — You decide if the reasons really back up the position, and you look at more than one side before deciding.
column14: Proficient — You decide if the reasons back up the position, and you point to evidence for why you think so.
column16: Progressing — You say what you think about the reasons, but you don't show much evidence for it.
column18: Beginning — You give your opinion without looking at the reasons yet.

column4: Create and use research questions to guide inquiry on an issue or event.
column5: Asking questions that drive research
column12: Exemplary — You write questions that open real research, and you change them as you find new information.
column14: Proficient — You write focused research questions and use them to guide your search.
column16: Progressing — You write questions, but they're too big, too small, or you set them aside once you start.
column18: Beginning — You name a topic without turning it into a question yet.

column4: Evaluate the breadth, reliability, and credibility of primary and secondary sources to determine the need for new or additional information when researching an issue or event.
column5: Judging whether sources can be trusted
column12: Exemplary — You judge whether a source can be trusted, and you notice what's missing or one-sided in what you found.
column14: Proficient — You judge whether a source can be trusted, and whether you need to find more.
column16: Progressing — You say something about your sources, but you judge them by how they look, not by who made them.
column18: Beginning — You use sources without asking where they came from yet.

column4: Engage in discussion, analyzing multiple viewpoints on public issues.
column5: Discussing an issue from more than one side
column12: Exemplary — You analyze several viewpoints in discussion and build on what others say, including views unlike yours.
column14: Proficient — You analyze more than one viewpoint on the issue while discussing it.
column16: Progressing — You take part in discussion, mostly restating one viewpoint.
column18: Beginning — You share an opinion without taking on the other views raised yet.

column3: SSS4: Creates a product that uses social studies content to support a thesis, and presents the product in an appropriate manner to a meaningful audience.

column4: Analyze multiple factors, make generalizations, and interpret sources to formulate a thesis in a paper or presentation, while observing rules related to plagiarism and copyright.
column5: Building a product that makes a claim
column12: Exemplary — All the parts build one idea together, and your idea says something people wouldn't guess right away.
column14: Proficient — Every part of your work supports the same clear claim.
column16: Progressing — Your parts connect to your claim, but some repeat or drift off it.
column18: Beginning — Your parts don't add up to a claim yet.

column4: Use appropriate format to cite sources within an essay, presentation, and reference page.
column5: Crediting sources correctly
column12: Exemplary — You cite sources the same way all the way through, and your citations make each source easy to find.
column14: Proficient — You cite your sources in the right format, both in your work and on your reference page.
column16: Progressing — You credit sources, but the format changes or your reference page is missing pieces.
column18: Beginning — You use other people's words or ideas without crediting them yet.
